faqs.q: There is a raccoon denning above my Manning ceiling. Will you release it somewhere wild?
faqs.a: We cannot promise a release, because the state does not allow routine relocation — a captured raccoon must be destroyed or moved only under a separate department permit. What works in Manning is getting the animal out and keeping the next one out: one-way eviction doors, removal under depredation rules where needed, and steel sealing at the roofline. Because raccoons lead SC Department of Public Health rabies results, we also treat attic contamination seriously and clean latrine spots rather than leaving them sealed in.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Manning home. Should I be worried?

Keep distance, bring pets in, and tell us the size, pattern, and where it sheltered. We identify from photos or on site, handle non-listed snakes where appropriate, and treat venomous encounters as safety work. Reducing cover and rodent food near the foundation lowers repeat sightings more than any single capture.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in Manning actually involve?

faqs.q: We found an opossum in our Summerton crawlspace. What happens next?

We trap at the access point, remove the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and seal the full foundation line. Securing pet food and trash at night removes the other half of the attraction.

Postwar brick and frame homes, lake and river cottages, and newer subdivisions share the same streets, with pine canopy hanging over most roofs. Hot summers and mild winters keep Midlands wildlife moving most of the year, and the spring litter season turns small roof gaps into denning calls within weeks.

Removal without repair does not hold in Summerton, so our visits pair the animal work with sealing and screening sized to the house itself.

faqs.q: There is a dead animal smell in my Turbeville walls. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call us rather than opening walls at random. Our crew locates the carcass — a dead raccoon, opossum, or squirrel in a wall void or crawlspace is the usual source — removes it, and sanitizes the area. Carcasses of raccoons, skunks, and bats are handled with rabies precautions in line with Department of Public Health guidance, and we check how the animal got in so the entry is sealed as part of the same visit.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Turbeville attics?
faqs.a: Gray squirrels need an opening little more than an inch wide, and the usual doors here are soffit corners, gable vents, and the gaps where additions meet the main roof, reached from fences and overhanging limbs. Trapping without sealing just invites the next squirrel, so our crew fits one-way doors, lets the animals leave, and seals every opening in steel — timed so a nursing litter is never sealed inside.

faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around Paxville?
faqs.a: Yes. Nine-banded armadillos are established throughout the entirety of South Carolina, and around here they burrow under porches, driveways, and crawlspace edges and root up lawns hunting grubs and worms. We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Alcolu home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.
